result: Italy has a national mandate for regions to implement organized population-based screening programs for breast, cervical, and colorectal cancer according to recommendations from the European Commission and Italian Ministry of Health.
evaluation: Claims C1, C15, and C28 consistently describe the Italian health policy framework for cancer screening. These are factual statements about the legal and organizational structure, supported by citations to Italian legislation (C15) and describing established knowledge about the Italian health system (C1, C28).

result: The COVID-19 pandemic in Italy began with the first diagnosis on February 20, 2020, followed by a strict lockdown from March 8 to early May 2020 that stopped all nonessential activities. Restrictions were gradually removed through June 2020, with relatively low incidence during summer, followed by a second wave starting in October with regionally-variable restrictions through December 2020.
evaluation: Claims C2, C21-C22, C25-C27, C29-C30, C32-C35 provide a consistent timeline of COVID-19 and control measures in Italy during 2020. These claims are supported by multiple citations to peer-reviewed studies and are consistent with publicly available data on the Italian pandemic response. The timeline is coherent and well-documented.

result: The first COVID-19 wave had a very strong impact in terms of deaths concentrated in Northern Italy, while a second wave starting in October 2020 involved all Italian regions.
evaluation: Claims C23 and C24 describe the geographic and temporal distribution of COVID-19 mortality in Italy. These claims are directly supported by mortality data presented in Figure 1, which shows clear geographic patterns of mortality across Italian regions during the two waves.

result: Before the COVID-19 pandemic, Italian screening programs showed geographic variation with near-complete invitation coverage in Central Italy and for breast cancer in Northern Italy, but incomplete coverage for colorectal screening in Southern Italy. Test coverage reached 75%, 80%, and 48% for breast, cervical, and colorectal cancers respectively, with opportunistic screening contributing about one-fourth, one-third, and one-sixth of coverage.
evaluation: Claims C16-C20 describe pre-pandemic baseline screening coverage in Italy. These claims are supported by historical data from the ONS monitoring system and cited studies (C19, C20). The geographic patterns and coverage levels are consistent with the Italian screening program structure and provide necessary context for evaluating pandemic impact.

result: During the second wave (October-December 2020), Italy implemented a color-coded regional restriction system based on epidemiological indicators. While official measures did not mandate reduction of nonurgent health services and some regions included cancer screening among services to maintain, hospital pressure in many areas necessitated reducing nonurgent activities to redirect health professionals to COVID-19 care.
evaluation: Claims C36-C41 describe the restriction system during the second wave. The color-coded system is documented (C36), and the discrepancy between official policy (C38-C39) and actual implementation (C40) is explicitly acknowledged. This nuanced description of policy versus practice is appropriately characterized as inference (C40) and reflects the complexity of pandemic response.

result: All 21 Italian regions participated in the ONS survey. Despite national directives to suspend screening first-level activities while maintaining diagnostic assessment, the suspension was heterogeneous across regions. Most programs restarted in May/June 2020 with reduced capacity (30-50% fewer exams per hour due to infection control measures), and many programs reduced invitation pace during the autumn 2020 second wave.
evaluation: Claims C42-C50 describe the qualitative findings from the ONS survey regarding screening program suspension and restart. The heterogeneity in implementation (C44-C45) is well-documented, and the capacity reductions due to infection control measures (C48) are specific and plausible. The complete regional participation (C42) strengthens the representativeness of the findings.

result: In 2020 compared to 2017-2019, screening invitations decreased for all three cancers in Northern and Southern Italy, with Central Italy maintaining the best performance (near 100% for cervical, just below 90% for breast and colorectal). The reduction was large and consistent across all macro areas during January-September 2020. In October-December 2020, Central Italy attempted catch-up, Northern Italy continued pre-pandemic pace, while Southern Italy continued reduced activity through Q1 2021.
evaluation: Claims C3, C51-C55 describe quantitative ONS survey findings on invitation coverage. The geographic and temporal patterns are clearly documented in Figures 2 and 3. The differential recovery patterns by region (C54-C55) are specific and supported by the data. The complete regional participation (C42) ensures these findings are nationally representative.

result: The reduction in examination coverage was larger than the reduction in invitation coverage for all screening programs and macro areas in 2020 compared to 2017-2019, indirectly indicating decreased participation. In Central and Northern Italy, test reductions were strongest initially then gradually decreased, reaching pre-pandemic levels for breast and colorectal (but not cervical) screening by Q1 2021. In Southern Italy, reductions persisted through Q1 2021 for cervical and breast screening.
evaluation: Claims C4, C56-C58, C105 describe examination coverage findings from the ONS survey. The inference that larger examination than invitation reductions indicates decreased participation (C105) is reasonable and explicitly acknowledged as indirect evidence. The geographic and temporal patterns are supported by Figure 3 data. The differential recovery by cancer type and region is well-documented.

result: The cumulative delay in screening the target population through May 2021 differed by macro area, being larger in Southern Italy and smaller in Central Italy. Within Northern and Central Italy, some regions accumulated negligible delays (<45 days) while others accumulated approximately 1 year of delay across all programs.
evaluation: Claims C59-C60 describe the calculated 'standard months of delay' metric from the ONS survey, presented in Table 2. The extreme variability between regions within macro areas (C60) is particularly notable and well-documented. This metric provides a clear quantification of the backlog accumulated during the pandemic.

result: PASSI survey data showed a clear decrease in test coverage for mammographic and colorectal screenings starting from the second half of 2020 across all macro areas. The decrease was smaller for cervical cancer screening due to longer screening intervals reducing the impact of the disruption period. Stopping screening programs and their slow restart caused an appreciable decrease in test coverage for breast and colorectal cancer in the target population.
evaluation: Claims C5, C61-C62, C106-C107 describe PASSI survey findings on population-level test coverage. The temporal patterns are clearly shown in Figure 4. The explanation for smaller cervical cancer impact (C107) is logical given the 3-5 year screening intervals versus 1-2 years for breast and colorectal. The PASSI data complement the ONS program-level data by capturing population-level coverage including opportunistic screening.

result: In 2020, there was an inversion of a long-term trend, with a decrease in opportunistic screening in favor of organized screening for cervical cancer.
evaluation: Claim C63 describes a trend reversal for cervical cancer screening shown in Figure 5. This finding is notable as it suggests the pandemic differentially affected opportunistic versus organized screening. The visual evidence in Figure 5 clearly supports this claim.

result: Opportunistic screening did not mitigate the pandemic's impact. For colorectal screening, opportunistic screening contribution was negligible before and during the pandemic. For breast and cervical cancer, opportunistic screening did not increase population test coverage, with only a small peak of women reporting paid tests during the March-May 2020 strict lockdown.
evaluation: Claims C9, C108-C110 address whether opportunistic screening compensated for organized screening disruption. The PASSI data in Figure 8 clearly show no compensatory increase in opportunistic screening. The small peak during strict lockdown (C110) is appropriately characterized as minor. This is a key finding demonstrating that organized screening disruption directly translated to reduced population coverage.

result: Compared with the pre-pandemic period, there was a greater difference according to educational level in the odds of having had a test in the last year. The decrease in test coverage was steeper in people with lower educational level. Multivariate Poisson models showed the probability of having a test in the last year was lower in 2020 even when adjusting for other variables, with larger differences by education level in 2020 than pre-pandemic for all three screenings.
evaluation: Claims C6, C64, C67-C68, C77 describe increased educational inequalities during the pandemic. While the Poisson models (Tables 3-4) and trend data (Figure 6) support these patterns, the authors explicitly acknowledge that differences could be due to random fluctuations (C68). The wide confidence intervals in Table 4 for 2020 education effects suggest limited statistical power. The finding is plausible and consistent with the data, but the uncertainty is appropriately noted.

result: For breast cancer screening, foreigners had a lower probability of having had a test than Italians in 2020, inverting the pre-pandemic pattern. Differences disadvantaging immigrants that were small in previous years became larger in 2020. This may reflect that immigrants rely mostly on organized screening and scarcely on opportunistic screening for mammography. People with lower education and immigrants experienced the largest lack of access to secondary prevention during the pandemic.
evaluation: Claims C69, C78-C79, C112 describe increased inequalities for immigrants, particularly for breast cancer. The Poisson models (Table 3) show the pattern reversal for breast cancer. However, the explanation (C79) is explicitly characterized as speculative, and the confidence intervals in Table 4 are wide. The finding is plausible and important for health equity, but the evidence is less definitive than for other results. The claim about immigrants experiencing the largest lack of access (C112) may overstate the certainty given the statistical limitations.

result: Differences by age and economic difficulties remained substantially unchanged in the pandemic compared with the pre-pandemic period.
evaluation: Claim C70 describes the stability of age and economic difficulty effects across periods. This is supported by the Poisson regression models in Tables 3-4, where the effect sizes for these variables are similar in 2017-2019 and 2020 periods. This finding provides important context that not all inequalities increased during the pandemic.

result: The pandemic increased preexisting individual and geographical inequalities in access to screening. The differential recovery across regions increased already existing geographical inequalities. The decrease in test coverage provided by organized screening programs caused an increase in inequalities.
evaluation: Claims C8, C76, C91, C111 represent the main conclusion about increased inequalities. These are supported by the convergence of evidence from ONS data (geographic inequalities in delay accumulation, Table 2) and PASSI data (socioeconomic inequalities in coverage, Figures 6-7, Tables 3-4). The inference that organized screening disruption caused increased inequalities (C111) is reasonable given that organized programs serve disadvantaged populations who lack access to opportunistic screening.

result: The lockdown and ongoing COVID-19 emergency caused an important delay in screening activities. Catch-up of backlog differed across regions and cannot be explained by pandemic severity in different areas. The resilience of screening programs seems to reflect the historical robustness of the organization, with areas achieving higher pre-pandemic invitation and test coverage reacting more promptly to the COVID-19 crisis.
evaluation: Claims C7, C89-C90 represent key interpretive conclusions. The delay is well-documented by ONS data (C7). The inference that differences cannot be explained by pandemic severity (C89) is supported by comparing Figure 1 (mortality patterns) with Table 2 and Figure 3 (recovery patterns) - Northern Italy had high mortality but variable recovery. The interpretation about historical robustness (C90) is appropriately characterized as inference and is consistent with the data showing Central Italy (historically strong programs) had better recovery.

result: The COVID-19 pandemic and control measures impacted health services and prevention behaviors globally. Cancer screening tests were among the first suspended activities in most European countries. However, organized screening programs' active invitation system allows accurate workload planning, representing an opportunity for rational post-lockdown resumption. Structured, well-organized programs have been recognized as favoring health service resilience to pandemic disruption.
evaluation: Claims C10-C14 provide literature-based context for the study. These claims are supported by multiple citations to peer-reviewed studies and describe established knowledge about pandemic impacts on health services and the theoretical advantages of organized screening programs. This context appropriately frames the Italian findings.

result: Other studies reported early disruption of screening activities following lockdown with reduced participation upon restart, showing large differences across countries in programs' ability to resume and catch up. Italy's federal health system with regional implementation resulted in extreme variability in cumulative delay during the COVID-19 emergency. Some areas recovered all backlog while most continued accumulating delay through early 2021.
evaluation: Claims C71-C75 contextualize Italian findings within international literature and explain variability through Italy's federal structure. The international comparison (C71-C72) is supported by citations. The explanation of Italian variability through federal structure and historical differences (C73-C74) is appropriately characterized as inference supported by citation. The differential recovery (C75) is directly supported by ONS data in Table 2 and Figure 3.

result: Studies from the US showed increased inequalities consequent to screening program interruption, with larger impact in rural areas and for beneficiaries of public insurance or uninsured individuals.
evaluation: Claim C80 provides international comparison for the inequality findings. This is supported by citations to US studies and provides important context that increased inequalities during pandemic screening disruption were observed in other countries with different health systems.

result: Many studies from Italy and other countries reported delays in cancer diagnoses across multiple sites. Some studies observed shifts to more advanced stages and different initial therapeutic approaches for breast and colorectal cancers.
evaluation: Claims C81-C82 describe downstream consequences of screening delays reported in the literature. These are supported by multiple citations and provide important context for the potential health impact of the documented screening disruptions. However, the manuscript does not directly assess stage at diagnosis or treatment approaches.

result: Modeling studies estimate screening disruption will increase cancer-specific mortality: 8-10% for breast cancer and 15-17% for colorectal cancer over 5 years in England assuming 12-month suspension. Simulation models suggest 1-3% relative increase in breast and colorectal cancer mortality over 10-30 years depending on disruption duration and catch-up strategies. For cervical cancer, a 6-month delay could lead to 600 additional cancers in the next screening round without catch-up. Similar impacts are expected in Italy given the observed 6-month average delay.
evaluation: Claims C83-C88 discuss potential health impacts based on modeling studies from other countries. While the cited models (C83, C85-C87) are appropriately referenced, the extrapolation to Italy (C88) is speculative. The Italian context differs in several ways: (1) extreme regional variability in delay (Table 2) versus assumed uniform delays in models, (2) heterogeneous catch-up efforts, (3) different baseline screening performance. The authors appropriately characterize these as expectations rather than predictions, but the uncertainty in applying these models to the Italian context should be emphasized. Additionally, the manuscript does not present original modeling or validation of these estimates for Italy.

result: National directives recommended maintaining diagnostic assessment for those who tested positive and assuring oncological follow-up. Assessment of people who had previously had a positive screening test was never stopped in any program.
evaluation: Claims C31 and C46 describe the continuity of diagnostic assessment and follow-up during the pandemic. C31 is supported by citations to official directives, and C46 is based on qualitative ONS survey data. This finding is important as it shows that while screening was disrupted, the diagnostic pathway for those already identified as positive was maintained.

result: The PASSI surveillance system had an 80% response rate during 2017-2020 and provides information on test coverage including both organized and opportunistic screening, with data on socio-demographic characteristics. Lombardy suspended PASSI surveillance in 2016, and Piedmont data were excluded from colorectal screening analyses due to different screening test (flexosigmodoscopy once in life).
evaluation: Claims C92-C96 describe the PASSI survey methodology and data limitations. The 80% response rate (C92) is good for a telephone survey. The exclusions (C95-C96) are appropriately documented and justified. These methodological details are important for interpreting the PASSI findings, particularly the exclusion of Lombardy, which was heavily affected by COVID-19.

result: The 'standard months of delay' metric represents the number of months required to catch up with cumulative backlog if programs screened at pre-COVID pace. This is calculated by multiplying the percent reduction in tests performed during the study period compared to 2019 by the duration in months of the study period.
evaluation: Claims C97-C98 define and explain the calculation of a key outcome metric. The definition is clear and the calculation method is straightforward. This metric provides an intuitive way to quantify the backlog accumulated during the pandemic. However, it assumes constant pre-pandemic screening pace and does not account for potential catch-up strategies that might increase pace above baseline.
